intro: Cagliari's biggest tree stands outside the central railway station: a Moreton Bay fig twelve metres round, fenced at the base. A second fig, 9.8 metres round, holds the corner where Via Roma meets the waterfront. The Giardini Pubblici, Sardinia's oldest park, adds twinned figs, a honey locust and a jacaranda, and the botanical garden nearby holds a third fig, an ombu, a dragon tree and an argan, the only one in an Italian garden. Further out: a Pirri cypress, two Dolianova pines, and a blue gum and lime above Sinnai. Ten of fourteen stand within a kilometre and a half.
meta_description: Cagliari's monumental trees: a fig twelve metres round outside the station, another on the Via Roma waterfront, and three in Sardinia's oldest park.
question_meta: Cagliari's oldest tree is the cypress in the Pirri cemetery, over two hundred years old and older than the graveyard. Where it stands, plus twelve more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Cagliari is the cypress in the Pirri cemetery, which Sardinian press covering its 2025 protection puts at more than two hundred years old: it was already standing when the burial ground was consecrated in November 1913. The only tree here that comes close is the Tintitaco in the Parco della Rimembranza, and its own record disagrees with itself, roughly 166 years on the Italian tree registry against about 200 in local reporting. The figs are younger than both. The two on the city squares are given 140 to 150 years, and the pair in the Giardini Pubblici anywhere between 140 and 195, a range nobody has narrowed.
question_context: Ages are the soft part of the record in Cagliari. Italy's national register of monumental trees, which covers most trees on this page, measures girth and height but carries no age field. Three of the four botanical garden trees carry no register entry; their ages come instead from the garden's own account of which specimens date from its 1866 founding, held to a wide band (the fourth, the argan, is not part of that founding-era account and carries no age at all). Every other year here comes from local and regional newspapers, council designation notices, or the independent Italian tree registry, the only source to date the Tintitaco. Where sources disagree, this page gives both figures. Access is simpler for most. Ten of fourteen stand on free public ground; six of those sit within a kilometre and a half in the centre, alongside the botanical garden's four paid trees, the rest reached by bus, regional train or car into the hills above Sinnai. A precautionary fence rings the station fig, and the Pirri cypress sits in a working cemetery with visiting hours. Two further register trees were checked and left off: both on private ground.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cagliari?
faq.a: The cypress in the Pirri cemetery, put at over two hundred years old by regional press. It was already growing on the site when the cemetery was consecrated in 1913.

faq.q: What is the biggest tree in Cagliari?
faq.a: The Moreton Bay fig on Piazza Matteotti, outside the central railway station, with a trunk twelve metres round on the national register's measurement. The fig on Via Roma is next at 9.8 metres.

faq.q: Why is the fig outside the station fenced off?
faq.a: As a precaution against branch drop, since November 2025. A University of Sassari assessment in January 2025 found no risk of structural collapse, and the city says the tree is healthy and under continuous management. You can stand beside it but not under the crown.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Ten of the fourteen, yes. The station fig, the Via Roma fig, the Tintitaco, the three Giardini Pubblici trees and the four in the university's botanical garden all sit within about a kilometre and a half of each other. The Pirri cypress is four kilometres out and needs a bus. Dolianova's two pines are further still, an 18km train ride, and both the blue gum near Sinnai and the lime at Corongiu are car-only trips into the hills above town; each makes its own separate day out.

trees.name: The Ficus of Piazza Matteotti

location.address: Piazza Giacomo Matteotti, Cagliari (in front of Cagliari's central railway station)
location.neighbourhood: Marina, opposite the port and central station

trees.story:
Twelve metres around the trunk. That is the largest girth Italy's national register of monumental trees records for any tree in Cagliari, and it belongs to a fig from the far side of the world standing on the square outside the central railway station.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the coastal forests of eastern Australia, and at this size it stops behaving like a street tree. Aerial roots come down from the limbs, thicken where they meet the ground and fuse into a base with no clean edge to put a tape around. Local reporting puts the tree at 140 to 150 years old.

The fence is the first thing a visitor notices. The city ringed the ground under the canopy in November 2025 as a precaution against branch drop, so you can stand beside the tree but not walk under it. It is not a sign of decline. A University of Sassari team assessed the trunk in January 2025 with a dendrodensimeter, an instrument that reads the density of the wood as it drills, and reported no risk of structural collapse and no damage from the building works going on in the piazza. In April 2026 the councillor responsible for the city's green spaces said the same thing plainly: the tree is healthy, and has been under continuous technical management since 2019.
verified_sources: https://www.cagliaritoday.it/cronaca/ficus-monumentale-sta-bene-parla-giua-marassi.html (23 April 2026, fetched via curl with browser user agent, WebFetch itself 403s this host)
MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 03/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free, public square; a temporary precautionary fence currently rings the ground beneath the canopy (branch-drop risk), so visitors can see and stand near the tree but not walk directly under the crown
trees.transport: Directly outside Cagliari's central railway station (Stazione di Cagliari); city buses converge on the piazza
trees.verify_notes: Height 22.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 12 metres round with no clean edge where aerial roots have fused into the base, now ringed by a precautionary fence. It stands in Piazza Matteotti.

trees.name: The Ficus of Piazza Ingrao

location.address: Piazza F.P. Ingrao, at the junction of Via Roma, Via Regina Margherita and Via XX Settembre, Cagliari

trees.story:
Local press calls this the fig that survived the bombs. Cagliari was hit hard from the air in 1943 and the Moreton Bay fig on the corner where Via Roma meets Via Regina Margherita came through it, which is a large part of why the city is fond of it.

CagliariNews dates the planting to about 1883, when the harbour front was being laid out as the Parterre della Darsena, so the tree is over 140 years old. Italy's national register of monumental trees measures the trunk at 9.8 metres round, second in the city only to the fig outside the railway station, five minutes west along the same waterfront.

Sardinia added it to the regional list of monumental trees on 21 January 2025, on the same day as the cypress in the Pirri cemetery. The case local reporting made for it was not only age. A canopy this size over one of Cagliari's busiest junctions cools the air under it, takes in what the traffic puts out, and holds resident and migrating birds through the year. It is a working tree in a place that badly needs one, and the fact that it is Australian, like every other big fig in this city, has stopped being remarkable to anybody who lives here.
verified_sources: MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 09/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free, public square on the Via Roma waterfront
trees.transport: 5-10 minutes' walk from Piazza Matteotti / the central railway station, along Via Roma
trees.verify_notes: Height 20.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 9.8 metres round, the city's second largest fig. It stands where Via Roma meets Via Regina Margherita, five minutes from the station fig.

trees.name: The Twin Figs of Giardini Pubblici

location.address: Giardini Pubblici, main entrance at Largo Giuseppe Dessi / Via Badas (end of Viale Regina Elena), Cagliari
location.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega

trees.story:
The national register does not measure these two figs separately. It files them as an insieme omogeneo, a homogeneous group, which is how they read from the path: two Moreton Bay figs of much the same size and age, standing together on the avenue near the main entrance of the Giardini Pubblici.

They are the quieter half of Cagliari's fig story. The park opened between 1866 and 1873 on ground the city had used for its bastion and its lazzaretto, which makes it the oldest public park in Sardinia, and these two went in early enough that published estimates of their age start at 140 years and run as far as 195. Nobody has narrowed that. The city's own pages and the local press cite different figures and neither has been withdrawn.

In November 2021 the council put three of the park's trees onto the Sardinian regional list of monumental trees: this pair and the honey locust a short walk away. Regional money followed, earmarked for maintenance on the park's protected trees. What that buys is time. A Ficus macrophylla at this size carries limbs longer than most trees are tall, drops aerial roots from them and thickens the ones that reach soil into props, and keeping that structure standing over a public path is the whole job.
trees.how_to_recognise: The pair of big figs standing together on the avenue near the main entrance. The honey locust and the jacaranda are elsewhere in the park and are far lighter, more open trees.
verified_sources: MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 07/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk (Comune di Cagliari, Sardinia's oldest public park)
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne

trees.name: The Spino di Giuda of Giardini Pubblici

location.address: Giardini Pubblici, Viale Regina Elena, Cagliari
location.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega

trees.story:
Italians call this species spino di Giuda, Judas's thorn, and the local name for this particular tree sometimes adds inerme: thornless. That is the joke of it. A wild Gleditsia triacanthos defends itself with branched spines that grow in bunches straight out of the trunk, long enough to go through a boot. The form planted in parks has had them bred out.

It is the third of the three Giardini Pubblici trees Cagliari's council put onto the Sardinian regional list of monumental trees in November 2021, alongside the pair of Moreton Bay figs a short walk away, and by some distance the least obvious of them. The national register measured its trunk at 2.94 metres round in 2020 and nobody has taped it since. No source gives it a documented age; the figures that circulate for the park's protected trees put it somewhere over a century, and that is as close as the record comes.

Honey locust is a tree of central North America and it does not look like the figs at all. The leaves are pinnate and small enough to read as ferns from underneath, they come late and go early, and the seed pods are long, dark and twisted, hanging in the crown well after the leaves have gone.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the Giardini Pubblici, a three-metre trunk under small fern-like leaves and long twisted seed pods. Not one of the figs, which are several times heavier at the base.
verified_sources: MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 06/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne
trees.verify_notes: Height 15.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: The Jacaranda of Giardini Pubblici

location.address: Giardini Pubblici, Viale Regina Elena, Cagliari
location.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega

trees.story:
For a few weeks each May this tree stops being green. Jacaranda mimosifolia flowers in violet-blue trumpets across the entire crown, and what falls carpets the ground beneath it in the same colour, which is why the species has been planted in warm cities from Pretoria to Lisbon to Sydney.

It is the odd one out among the Giardini Pubblici's protected trees, and much the smallest: Italy's national register of monumental trees gives it 1.74 metres round and 16 metres tall, against figs that go to twelve. Its record is also the thinnest here. That register is the only source that has measured this tree on its own, and when regional funding for maintenance of the park's monumental trees came round in 2025 the coverage named the jacaranda without adding an age or a condition report specific to it. So the century or more given on this page is an estimate in line with the trees standing around it, not a dated figure, and it should be read that way.

The species comes from the dry forests of northwestern Argentina and Bolivia. It flowers on bare or barely-leafed branches, which is what produces the effect: no green to dilute it, just the whole shape of the tree in one colour for a fortnight.
trees.how_to_recognise: The smallest of the park's protected trees, under two metres round, and the only one that flowers violet-blue. Out of flower, look for fine fern-like foliage.

best_time.label: May, when the whole crown turns violet-blue

verified_sources: MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 01/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne
trees.verify_notes: Height 16.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: The Tintitaco

location.address: Parco della Rimembranza, Via Sonnino, Cagliari

trees.story:
This tree has no English name. Sardinians call it the tintitaco, the Italian tree registry that keeps the fullest record of it translates that as the Admiral's Tree, and Prosopis torquata, a thorny mesquite from the dry country of northwestern Argentina, is otherwise close to unknown in European parks.

The name points at the story local sources tell. An English naval commander, a ship that put into Cagliari to sit out a storm with a cargo of exotic plants, and this one left behind as a gift to the city. It is repeated in several places and documented in none, so read it as the city's own account rather than as a record.

The measurements come with the same caution. The national register lists the trunk at 3 metres round; the Italian tree registry gives 5.7 metres, taken at ground level because the trunk divides low, at about 1.3 metres. Both are right at the height they were measured. Age splits the same way: roughly 166 years on the registry's most recent update, around 200 in local reporting, and no figure at all on the national sheet.

The state of it is not in dispute. One heavy limb rests on scaffolding and a metal cage holds the trunk on one side. It is alive, protected under Sardinian law, and very obviously being kept that way.

trees.access: Free, public park (Parco della Rimembranza / Parco delle Rimembranze), open daily
trees.transport: Roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from the city centre, or a short bus ride to Via Sonnino
trees.verify_notes: Height 17.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (1 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, thorny trunk dividing near ground level, propped on scaffolding and caged on one side. It stands in the Parco della Rimembranza on Via Sonnino.

trees.name: The Cypress of Pirri Cemetery

location.address: Cimitero di Pirri, Via Gioachino Murat, Cagliari

trees.story:
The cemetery came second. Pirri's burial ground was consecrated on 8 November 1913 and this cypress was already standing on the site, more than two hundred years old by the reckoning of the Sardinian press that covered its protection in 2025.

That makes it, on the published figures, the oldest tree on this page. It is also improbably heavy for its species. Italy's national register of monumental trees puts the trunk at 6.3 metres round, where a Mediterranean cypress normally goes up as a narrow dark column and stays that way for centuries.

Cupressus sempervirens has been the tree of Mediterranean burial grounds since long before this one was planted: evergreen, so it never looks dead, and slow enough to outlast everyone buried beneath it. The unusual part here is the order of events. This tree did not arrive to mark the graves, the graves arrived around the tree, and generations of Pirri residents have used it as a landmark rather than a monument.

Sardinia added it to the regional list of monumental trees on 21 January 2025, the same day as the fig on Via Roma. Pirri is a district about four kilometres out from the old centre, on a city bus route, and this is a working cemetery rather than a garden: visiting hours, quiet, and people there with a reason.
verified_sources: MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 08/B354/CA/20 (italy-masaf)
trees.access: Free, public municipal cemetery; open during standard cemetery visiting hours
trees.transport: Roughly 4 km from the historic centre; CTM city bus lines serve Pirri directly
trees.verify_notes: Height 15.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.3 metres round, unusually thick for a Mediterranean cypress. It stands inside the Pirri cemetery, older than the graves arranged around it.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pines of San Pantaleo
trees.access: Free, open piazza and cathedral churchyard
trees.transport: Regional train from Cagliari to Dolianova, about 23 minutes, then a short walk to the cathedral square
trees.notes: Day trip entry, 18km/23 min train from Cagliari centre, per the day-trip boundary rule. Two register entries (MASAF sheets 01/D323/CA/20 and 02/D323/CA/20) folded into one entry per the twin/group convention: the larger pine (girth 340cm, height 19.5m) stands in the open Piazza San Pantaleo; the smaller (girth 265cm, height 16.7m) stands inside the cathedral's own sagrato (walled forecourt) a short walk away on Via San Martino. Both are the Comune di Dolianova's own designated 'Bellezza naturale' landmarks, each with its own page explicitly stating public access ('libera e fruibile a tutti'). Age is the municipality's own register estimate, a band under 100 years, deliberately not sharpened.
trees.story:
Two Aleppo pines stand at the doorstep of one of Sardinia's most important Romanesque churches, in the small town of Dolianova, about 23 minutes from Cagliari by regional train. The larger, 3.4 metres round and just under 20 metres tall, grows in the open Piazza San Pantaleo, facing the cathedral's stone facade. The second, a metre smaller round, stands inside the sagrato, the walled forecourt where the cathedral keeps its own patch of ground.

The Concattedrale di San Pantaleo behind them was built between the early 1100s and 1289, one of the oldest and most complete Romanesque buildings on the island, its sandstone walls carved with the geometric and animal motifs typical of the period. The pines are far younger: Dolianova's own register puts each at under a century old, but they have grown up in the shadow of a building that predates them by 800 years, and the town has designated both as protected natural landmarks in their own right.

Both stand on open, unticketed ground, which the town's own listing describes in as many words as free and open to everyone. A short detour off any Cagliari itinerary, and a chance to see Italy's national register of monumental trees include something other than a giant.
trees.verify_notes: Height 19.5 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise the larger by its 3.4 metre trunk in the open piazza; the smaller stands a metre narrower inside the cathedral's walled forecourt. They stand at Piazza San Pantaleo, Dolianova.

trees.name: The Blue Eucalyptus of Campu Omu

location.address: Loc. Campu Omu, near the former Tavernetta E.S.I.T., Sinnai (edge of the Foresta dei Sette Fratelli), Sardinia

verified_sources: https://idese.cultura.gov.it/place/eucalipto-blu-di-campu-omu/ (Idese, the Ministero della Cultura's own Sardinia heritage portal)
MASAF national monumental trees register (italy-masaf, girth 520cm/height 30m at 39.35556,9.21999; sardinia-alberi-monumentali.json carries a duplicate entry at 39.35551,9.22014)
trees.access: Free entry, full motor accessibility per the Idese listing, parking on site, tree stands about 50m walk from the car park; no public transport reaches Campu Omu, a car is required (visible from the SS125 Orientale Sarda)
trees.transport: Car only, roughly 15km / 25-30 min drive northeast of Cagliari centre via the SS125, into the Foresta dei Sette Fratelli near Sinnai; no bus service to the site itself
trees.story:
Sardinia has almost no native eucalyptus, and that is the point of this one. Eucalyptus globulus, the Tasmanian blue gum, arrived on the island as a reforestation and windbreak species, planted along roads and forest edges rather than admired for its own sake. This one, standing at the edge of the Foresta dei Sette Fratelli near Sinnai, ended up on Italy's national register of monumental trees anyway, one of relatively few eucalyptus to make that list in a country where the species is functionally an immigrant.

The numbers disagree by about six percent, which for a tree this size is not much of an argument: the regional heritage portal measures the trunk at 4.9 metres round, the national register at 5.2, and both put the height at close to 30 metres. Age is recorded only loosely, as over a hundred years, which given how fast blue gums grow in the right climate could mean either a genuinely old specimen or one that simply had good conditions early.

The forest around it is real, a reserve for the Sardinian deer and for mouflon reintroduced here from the 1980s, and the tree stands a fifty metre walk from a car park with full public access and no entrance fee. There is no bus route out here. The road is the only way in, about half an hour from central Cagliari.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 5.2 metres round and 30 metres tall, one of Italy's few registered monumental eucalyptus. It stands at Campu Omu, on the edge of the Foresta dei Sette Fratelli.

trees.name: The Common Lime of Corongiu

location.address: Corongiu, near the historic Corongiu dams, Sinnai, Sardinia

trees.story:
Corongiu is three dams stacked up a valley above Sinnai, built between 1867 and 1922 to give Cagliari its first real water supply, and this lime tree has stood at the site for long enough that nobody now can say whether it predates the dams or came after them. At 2.6 metres round and 18 metres tall, it is the kind of specimen that only grows where a valley holds water and shelter both, which is exactly what an engineer would have looked for in 1867 too.

The reservoirs still work, still supply Cagliari, and the paths around them are now a public walking trail through the hills, popular enough that Legambiente and the water utility Abbanoa run organised visits explaining the site's history. Sardinia's own monumental tree register lists the lime by its measurements alone, no age, no planting story, just the girth and the height and the place name.

What that leaves unsettled is worth saying plainly: reach it on the open trail through the Corongiu valley, and whether that trail runs right up to the tree or past a fenced section of the works has not been confirmed. Anyone who has walked it can tell us, and settle the last honest gap in an otherwise well measured tree.
verified_sources: https://www.sardegnaforeste.it/sites/default/files/Elenco%20degli%20alberi%20monumentali%20della%20Sardegna.pdf (regional register, sheet 05/I752/CA/20, girth 260cm, height 18m, locality Corongiu, comune Sinnai)
trees.access: Free, no ticket; reached via the public walking trail through the historic Corongiu dam site above Sinnai (also used for organised Abbanoa/Legambiente visits). Whether the trail runs directly to the tree or past a fenced section of the waterworks was not confirmed; treat this as a walk to the site rather than a guaranteed close approach until a reader tells us more.
trees.transport: Car only, roughly 15-18km / 25-30 min drive northeast of Cagliari centre via Sinnai; no public transport reaches Corongiu

best_time.label: May to June, when it flowers

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 2.6 metres round and 18 metres tall, standing where the valley holds water and shelter both. It stands at the historic Corongiu dam site above Sinnai.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of the Orto Botanico
trees.age_estimate: over a century, among the garden's founding-era plantings

location.address: Orto Botanico di Cagliari, Viale Sant'Ignazio da Laconi 1, Cagliari

trees.story:
Cagliari's botanical garden was laid out in a valley the Romans had already used, on the site of an amphitheatre and a run of Punic and Roman cisterns, and it opened on 15 November 1866. This fig is one of the trees that went in at the start.

The date comes from the garden itself. Its account of its notable trees says they are the oldest specimens on the ground because they were planted during the founding phase, and it names this Ficus macrophylla in that list, alongside the ombu and the dragon tree. Allow the founding planting a decade or two beyond the opening and the fig comes out somewhere around 140 to 160 years old. Nobody has put a tape around it, so there is no girth to quote.

Cagliari's other Moreton Bay figs are public property in every sense: the giant on Piazza Matteotti outside the railway station, fenced off as a precaution and argued over in the local press, and the pair on the avenue in the Giardini Pubblici. This one has had the quieter life. It grew up inside a working university collection, on five hectares designed by the architect Gaetano Cima for the garden's first director Patrizio Gennari, among people whose job is to notice what trees do. Four euros gets you in, Monday to Saturday.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size and its big leathery evergreen leaves: it is the garden's one Moreton Bay fig. It stands apart from the ombu on the main avenue and from the dragon tree up by the department building.
trees.access: Paid entry, euro 4 (reduced/free for children under 6, over 65s, disabled visitors and school groups per italianbotanicalheritage.com). Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sundays and some public holidays.
trees.transport: In central Cagliari; about a 15 minute walk from the Giardini Pubblici cluster (cag_001-003), roughly 700m-1.2km from the other Piazza Matteotti/Ingrao figs (cag_004, cag_005).

trees.name: The Ombu of the Orto Botanico
trees.age_estimate: over a century, among the garden's founding-era plantings

location.address: Orto Botanico di Cagliari, Viale Sant'Ignazio da Laconi 1, Cagliari

trees.story:
The ombu is not built like a tree. Phytolacca dioica is a pachycaul, a plant that puts its bulk into a broad soft water-holding stem instead of into hard timber, which is how a South American relative of pokeweed ends up thickening at the base in a way no timber tree does.

Cagliari's grows along the main avenue of the botanical garden, past the bald cypresses and short of the Pampanini fountain, which is where the garden's own visitor route places it. Both the Italian parks and gardens association and the Italian Botanical Heritage survey list it among the garden's significant specimens, which is good company for a species most visitors would walk past without a second look.

Its age comes from the garden's own account, which says the notable trees are the oldest on the ground because they were planted during the founding phase, and names the Phytolacca dioica among them. The garden opened on 15 November 1866, so the ombu is up to about 160 years old, give or take however long that first planting ran on. What nobody has published is a girth, and on a trunk of this shape that is the measurement worth having. If you have stood beside it with a tape, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad swollen base of the trunk, unlike anything else growing here. It stands along the garden's main avenue, past the bald cypresses and before the Pampanini fountain.
trees.access: Paid entry, euro 4 (reduced/free for children under 6, over 65s, disabled visitors and school groups). Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sundays and some public holidays.
trees.transport: In central Cagliari; about a 15 minute walk from the Giardini Pubblici cluster (cag_001-003).

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of the Orto Botanico
trees.age_estimate: over a century, among the garden's founding-era plantings

location.address: Orto Botanico di Cagliari, near the Dipartimento di Scienze della Vita e dell'Ambiente building, Viale Sant'Ignazio da Laconi 1, Cagliari

trees.story:
Cut a dragon tree and it bleeds. The red resin that runs out is what gave Dracaena draco its name and what made the species worth shipping off the Canary Islands for centuries, as a dye, a varnish and a medicine.

This one stands near the Department of Botanical Sciences building at the top of Cagliari's botanical garden, and it is an odd thing to meet in Sardinia. Not a conifer and not a palm: a succulent that has worked out the shape of a tree, thickening slowly and dividing its crown into fistfuls of stiff sword-shaped leaves. The older it gets, the more branched and the more particular that crown becomes.

Dating one is hard, because a dragon tree lays down none of the annual rings you can count in an oak, and its age is usually read from how often the crown has forked. Here the figure comes from the garden instead. Its own account of its notable trees says they are the oldest specimens on the ground because they were planted during the founding phase, and it names the Dracaena draco in that list beside the ombu and the Moreton Bay fig. The garden opened on 15 November 1866 in the Valle di Palabanda, above Roman cisterns and the site of an amphitheatre, so this dragon tree has had up to about 160 years to build the head it carries now. Nobody has measured its trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stiff sword-shaped leaves bunched at the ends of thick pale branches, more succulent than tree. It stands near the Department of Botanical Sciences building at the top of the garden.
trees.access: Paid entry, euro 4 (reduced/free for children under 6, over 65s, disabled visitors and school groups). Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sundays and some public holidays.
trees.transport: In central Cagliari; about a 15 minute walk from the Giardini Pubblici cluster (cag_001-003).

trees.name: The Argan of the Orto Botanico

location.address: Orto Botanico di Cagliari, Viale Sant'Ignazio da Laconi 1, Cagliari

trees.access: Paid entry, euro 4 (reduced/free for children under 6, over 65s, disabled visitors and school groups). Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sundays and some public holidays. Same garden and terms as cag_011-013.
trees.transport: In central Cagliari, same site as cag_011-013 (the Moreton Bay Fig, Ombu and Dragon Tree of the Orto Botanico); about a 15 minute walk from the Giardini Pubblici cluster (cag_001-003).
trees.story:
Italy has exactly one argan tree in a botanical garden, and it grows in Cagliari.

Argania sideroxylon is endemic to the semi-arid south of Morocco and is planted almost nowhere in Europe. The Italian parks and gardens association lists this specimen as the only one in any Italian botanical garden. The Italian Botanical Heritage survey goes a step further and calls it probably the only one in any European botanical garden. A University of Bari research record on the species, written about something else entirely, agrees that the Cagliari tree is the only documented argan in the country.

So the reason to walk to this one is not age or size. It is that the species has no business being here at all. Argan is the tree behind argan oil, pressed from the kernels inside its fruit, and in its home range goats climb into the branches after them. Everything about it is built for drought: small leathery grey-green leaves, thorny branches, a crown that holds on through months without rain. Cagliari, hot and dry by the standards of anywhere north of it, is close enough to Morocco in climate to keep the tree alive.

The garden around it opened on 15 November 1866, on five hectares in the Valle di Palabanda above Punic and Roman cisterns. Nobody has published a planting date, an age or a girth for the argan itself. If you have measured it, or know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small leathery grey-green leaves and the thorny branches. It stands in the same five hectares as the Moreton Bay fig, the ombu and the dragon tree, and looks like none of the three.
